Pele Yoetz 288:1: Ayin HaRa (Evil Eye) — The evil eye is one of the things that remove a person from the world, and the well-known saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Bava Metzia 107b), is that ninety-nine die from the evil eye and one from natural causes. A person must guard himself greatly as much as he can — that is, that he not make himself conspicuous, neither in his wisdom nor in his deeds nor in his wealth; but he must be discreet so that people do not sense that he is guarding himself, lest they come to resent him for suspecting them of being possessors of the evil eye. And especially if he is a poor man and sees that a man who has grown rich is guarding himself from him, or one who is childless and sees that the father of children is guarding himself, they are crushed and their hearts ache and seized with pain — “and every shrewd man acts with knowledge” (Proverbs 13:16). And also let him not dwell upon his fellow's good fortune, nor sit in his shop, nor set his eyes upon it, nor speak of it, so that if some harm befalls it, it will not be attributed to him. And if it happens that conversation turns to mentioning his fellow's praise and good fortune, let him immediately bless him, so that the evil eye not have power over him.
Pele Yoetz 288:2: And the books already contain several remedies for being saved from the evil eye, and in particular the herb called “rodeh,” which is very effective to carry upon oneself, and it is fitting to follow them, for this is included in “and you shall greatly guard your souls” (Deuteronomy 4:15). And likewise, to be saved from one's own evil eye, it is stated in the Talmud (Berachot 55b) that there is a remedy: that he look with his eye at the left side of his nose. And above all, prayer bears fruit, for our God is merciful, hears the prayer of every mouth, and He is the one who saves His people Israel from the evil eye and from every evil thing. And in any case, one should not refrain from performing a commandment for fear of the evil eye, such as bringing a poor person into his house, or expounding publicly to teach the people knowledge, for one who guards a commandment shall know no evil thing, and a commandment protects and shields while one is engaged in it. And in the Talmud they said (ibid.) that one who fears the evil eye should say, “I come from the seed of Joseph, over whom the evil eye has no power,” etc., and it is good for a man to say this every day.
Pele Yoetz 289:1: Arayot (Forbidden Relations) — Israel is holy and few of them transgress in matters of forbidden relations, and they are exceedingly wary of the prohibition of forbidden relations, and especially those who dwell in the cities of Ishmael are more fenced in regarding forbidden relations. But there are lesser degrees of closeness to forbidden relations that people are not careful about — may the Good Name grant atonement for it, for the whole people acts in error. For they said (Shemot Rabbah 16:2) that woman is compared to a vine, as it is said, “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine” (Psalms 128:3). The Holy One, blessed be He, said: just as if a Nazirite vowed to abstain from wine, it is forbidden for him to eat fresh or dried grapes, or grape residue, or anything that comes from the grapevine of wine, so too a woman who is not yours is forbidden to touch at all, and whoever touches a woman who is not his brings death upon himself. And there they taught (Avot 1:5), “Whoever converses excessively with a woman brings evil upon himself, and in the end inherits Gehinnom.” And to what extent is the fence of “excessive conversation” drawn? To the point that they said (Eruvin 53b) that because Rabbi Yose the Galilean said to Beruriah, “By which way shall we go to Lod,” she called him “Galilean fool,” because he conversed excessively, since he could have said simply, “Which way to Lod?” And they said in the Talmud (Kiddushin 70a) that it is forbidden to make any use of a woman at all, whether grown or young, and in particular that she give him water to wash his face, his hands, or his feet, or fill his cup with wine or beer, or make his bed in his presence — this is a criminal offense, for a woman does these things only for her husband, or her father, or her son, and specifically while she is ritually pure. And likewise they said (ibid.) that a woman's voice is nakedness. And it is forbidden to greet a woman at all, and all these are settled halachot in the Talmud and the Shulchan Aruch (Even HaEzer, section 21).
Pele Yoetz 289:2: And the prohibition of gazing at women is exceedingly severe and is considered like licentiousness, as it is written (Numbers 15:39), “And you shall not go about after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray.” And this reincarnates into a bird called “ra'ah” [a bird of prey]. And Maimonides wrote that such a person is called an apostate in one matter, and of one who does not gaze at women the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “That is My judgment” [i.e., he judges as I do] (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:5). And the prohibition of gazing at women applies even if his heart is not inclined toward evil thoughts; nevertheless, the gazing itself damages the eyes of the soul, and through this our eyes have grown dark to seeing intellectual matters. And this is the natural inclination in a person, upon seeing a woman, to wish to look at her, and he must press himself and shut his eyes from seeing evil, and according to the pain is the reward.
Pele Yoetz 289:3: Now, regarding these matters of forbidden closeness that were said concerning strange women, it is relatively easy to be careful; but the difficult thing is to be careful regarding one's own relatives, and especially those who live together with him in the house, and all the more so since there is no one who is careful, for they do not know that there is a prohibition in the matter, and it has been treated as permitted. And one who wishes to be careful appears arrogant, saying to a woman that he does not wish to accept from her a vessel to wash his hands, or to accept the cup from her, and the like. But the man who fears the Name shall tremble and shrink from doing any hint of transgression whatsoever, and shall not turn back for anyone's sake, just as he would not worry about anything in order to be saved from losing a thousand thousand gold dinars — how much more so in order not to become liable for his own soul, and not to anger his Creator; this is a great principle in the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 289:4: And behold, regarding these prohibitions of closeness to forbidden relations, the women bear the primary portion, and they shall be disciplined with harsh afflictions and punishments, and their bitterness in Gehinnom, crying out with no one to save them, since they are the cause of damage in that they arouse the evil inclination in men, by going about among men and speaking excessive words with them. And even if the man is cleared of sin, having struggled with his inclination and been saved from actual transgression and from thoughts of transgression, that woman shall bear her own sin, and how much more so if she caused him to stumble into thoughts of transgression — woe to her, woe to her soul. And how much more so if men sing and women engage in matters of frivolous flirtation while adorned in finery, which is like fire in tow, may the Merciful One save us. Evil shall come upon these women, whether reward be evil, in this world or in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 289:5: And “a woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised” (Proverbs 31:30) — that she be careful and guard against causing anyone to stumble through any hindrance or sinful thought, and that she suspect every man as a robber in this matter, for there is no guardian against forbidden relations, and “whoever is greater than his fellow, his inclination is greater than his” (Sukkah 52b), and every impulse of the thoughts of his heart is only evil. And if he is a man, it is good that he struggle with his inclination and perhaps overcome it — but why should she bring this trouble upon him by entering into this contest? Therefore let a woman of valor be modest — “all the glory of the king's daughter is within” (Psalms 45:14) — then shall she delight in the Lord. And it is a commandment incumbent upon men to warn the women of his household that they be modest before all people.
Pele Yoetz 290:1: Edut (Testimony) — In several matters a person testifies about himself, and his witnesses either vindicate or condemn him. For example, if he says that his flesh pains him because he is not a Torah scholar, this shall be tested by whether he gives his life with all his strength and vigor so that his sons become Torah scholars. And if a person says that his soul is grieved that he does not have wealth so as not to be preoccupied with earning a livelihood and sustenance, and to be occupied only with Torah and Divine service, there is testimony to this: if on Shabbatot, festivals, and the intermediate days of festivals, and at every hour that he is free, he does not turn to idleness, but rather sits and studies and engages in the service of the blessed Name, then his words are trustworthy, and the Holy One, blessed be He, establishes reward for him — for such is His attribute, that if a person intended to perform a commandment and was prevented by circumstance beyond his control and did not perform it, Scripture accounts it to him as though he had performed it (Kiddushin 40a). And if they do not do so, but rather say, “When I am free I will study” (Avot 2:14), “He who sits in heaven shall laugh at them” (Psalms 2:4), and the early sages already explained by this the verse (ibid. 75:3), “When I take the appointed time, I shall judge with uprightness.”
Pele Yoetz 290:2: And there is further testimony: if he exerts all his efforts to support Torah scholars with his person and his money, so that they eat portion for portion equally. And if a person says that his soul is grieved that, because of our sins, the Holy Temple was destroyed, and we have neither altar nor priest to atone for us, there is testimony to this if his words are sincere and he does what stands in place of a sacrifice, such as performing charity and acts of kindness, studying the order of the sacrifices, and praying with intention, which he brings in place of a sacrifice. And one who brings a gift to a Torah scholar is as though he had offered first-fruits (Ketubot 105b), and one who wishes to offer libations should fill the throats of Torah scholars with wine (Yoma 71a). And a fast is considered like a sacrifice, and all kinds of suffering, if accepted with love, and all the more so if he afflicts himself with suffering and self-mortification as much as he can, is considered an atoning altar. And likewise there are several things that are effective to restrain transgression and to remove sin, like an atoning altar.
Pele Yoetz 290:3: And one who delights on Shabbat and says that his intention is for the sake of the commandment, for the honor of the holy Shabbat — there is testimony to this if he does not pursue the pleasures and vanities of this world during the weekdays. And if he fulfills the commandment of the third meal and the fourth meal even when he is full and has no appetite to eat at all, this is testimony that when he is hungry he also eats for the sake of the commandment. And likewise in this manner, if he fulfills commandments that involve affliction of the soul, this is testimony regarding commandments that involve delight of the soul, that he performs them for the sake of the commandment. Behold, we mention every day, always, the binding of Isaac, and perhaps a person will say, “I too, if the Holy One, blessed be He, said to me as He said to Abraham our father, I would do the same,” for indeed we intend in the Shema that we are ready to give our lives for the sanctification of the Name if the opportunity comes to us; but there is testimony to this — for “all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2:4), and if he transgresses his Maker's will for the sake of monetary gain, how much more so will he not give his life. And if he were to give his life not for the sake of Heaven, but because man's end is to die anyway, and he chooses a death for which he receives reward immediately, and his heart understands that through this he prepares himself for the life of the World to Come — that he does a great thing since the soul is dear — but if he truly loves the Lord, he will not transgress his Maker's will under any circumstance, and will not turn back from it even unto the utter dissolution of the soul; then it shall be accounted to him as though he gave his life for the sanctification of the Name, and He shall pay him his reward in full. And likewise if a person says that if he had wealth beyond measure he would perform wondrous acts of charity and kindness, the Name shall test him as to whether he does so with what he has, according to his measure, according to the blessing the Name has given him, as is fitting for him to do. And so in this manner, regarding all that a person says, his deeds are his witnesses, and the truth is with him if his actions are pure and upright.
Pele Yoetz 291:1: Atzeret (Shavuot) — Atzeret is an exceedingly holy festival, on which the blessed Name sanctified us with His Torah and commandments and chose us from among all the nations to be for Him a treasured people; and were it not for this day which caused it, we would have been like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah, and the statutes of heaven and earth would not have endured — in such a way that it is fitting to rejoice on this day. And it is impossible not to rejoice, for the goodness of Torah and commandments is better for us than all the good things of this world and all the life of the World to Come. And the reading of the Torah on the night of Atzeret, in the order arranged by our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, is wondrous and makes a great impression above, an adornment for the Divine Presence. Happy is one born of woman who has merited this, that the King of the world, awesome and fearsome, a great King whose greatness is beyond investigation, is likened, so to speak, in the works of His hands, and rides the heavens for our help, and Israel does valiantly and adds strength to the retinue on high. Over this let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad in his Maker, let the pious exult in glory and be occupied only with the order of study the entire night, without rest, with clear speech, with awe and love and abundant joy, more than one who finds abundant spoil, taking to heart what is done in the heavens above through us, and what these days are and what has reached us. And so, whoever does these things, behold his reward is with him: children who are sustained, long life, and ample sustenance, as it is written in the holy Zohar. And according to the greatness of the reward, from which we know that he creates great satisfaction above, let a man gather strength to remove sleep from his eyes and stay awake the entire night, provided that he does not sit idle or speak idle or forbidden words with one who raises smoke from his mouth [smokes], for if he does these things, the sleep [he forgoes] is a benefit to them and a benefit to the world; but the servants of the Lord who stand in the house of the Lord on this night unto the Lord must be occupied with Torah the entire night without interruption, and according to the pain is the reward, and it is a great rectification for the blemish of sight that he blemished by looking at forbidden sights, such as women and idols, and for having blemished several nights, toiling and being angry, staying awake to anger his Creator with laughter and levity and the like evils.
Pele Yoetz 291:2: And everything depends on the seal: that he strengthen himself like a lion to stay awake at the time of the Shema and prayer, for if he cannot manage this, it is better that he rest a little at night, or lie down the entire night and not recite the Shema and prayer while dozing. And let the righteous man hold to the paths of the righteous, to immerse in a mikveh of purity at the morning watch, for its secret is exalted and lofty, and it acquires illumination and sanctity and purity for his soul. And after prayer, let him eat rich foods and drink sweet drinks according to his ability, in honor of the day, for it is holy, and all agree that we also need “for yourselves” (Pesachim 68b). And after resting a little, let him return to his studies, for Torah is beloved, and especially at its own time, on the day it was given. And how good, a thing in its season, to pour out his soul in these days and at this time, that he and his sons merit the crown of Torah, to study and to teach, to observe and to do.
Pele Yoetz 292:1: The letter Peh: Perishut (Abstinence) — One who separates from transgression is as one who separates from death, and not only from transgression itself, but even from any hint of transgression whatsoever. For the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote regarding the coffee of the gentiles, and these are his words: “One who separates from it on a weekday is as one who separates from death, and one who separates from it on Shabbat shall merit the world that is entirely Shabbat.” And it is exceedingly bitter, more bitter than death, that a person, who is likened to vanity, should cause blemish and pain and anger before the King, exalted and lofty, awesome and fearsome, who dwells on high. Let the living take this to heart, let him not remove it from his eyes, and let him increase abstinence, and thereby his lamp shall shine and not be extinguished.
Pele Yoetz 293:1: Periyah U'Reviyah (Procreation) — Procreation is a great commandment, and happy are the Israelites dwelling in the cities of Ishmael, all of whom are careful about it — there are diligent ones who marry early and there are those who delay, but there is not even one who does not engage in procreation. But in the cities of Edom there are, indeed there are, those who do not marry and grow old and die like a shrub in the wilderness, pursuing vain and misleading burdens — woe to them and woe to their souls. For who is greater to us than King Hezekiah, who was a perfectly righteous man and increased and gathered laborers for Torah wondrously, and the reason he did not marry a woman was because he saw through the holy spirit that unworthy sons would issue from him; and even so, Isaiah the prophet came to him and said (II Kings 20:1), “Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.” And our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 10a): “You shall die” in this world, “and not live” in the World to Come. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yevamot 63b) that whoever does not engage in procreation is as though he diminishes the [divine] image, and as though he sheds blood, and causes the Divine Presence to depart from Israel, and is liable to death. And they further said (Yevamot 62b), “One who dwells without a wife dwells without blessing,” etc. And there are many more such statements of our sages, of blessed memory, in the Talmud, the Midrashim, and the holy Zohar. And certainly whoever is a Jew and believes in the Torah and in the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, will not deal falsely with his own soul and will not be one who destroys himself knowingly, from this world and from the World to Come. And these sinners against their own souls, who do not marry and do not engage in procreation, shall certainly be blotted out from the Book of Life and shall not rest upon their beds.
Pele Yoetz 293:2: And even if he has already married and fulfilled the commandment of procreation, if his wife dies he should not remain without a wife, but should marry a woman capable of bearing children, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (ibid.), “If he married in his youth, let him marry in his old age; if he had children in his youth, let him have children in his old age,” as it is said (Ecclesiastes 11:6), “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand, for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will be good.” And for this reason it is fitting for a person to make efforts with his wife and produce abundant offspring and engage in remedies even if he already has children, for perhaps the sun will shine for him from one who issued from his own loins, and one soul is a whole world, for Abraham was one and from him came forth all of Israel, among whom are several righteous and pious people — and not like those who err in understanding, who worry about the great trouble of children and the increasing expense of the household, and are pained if their wife bears many children, and content themselves with two or three children and do not wish for more. And would that they were wise and understood, for it is fitting to exert great effort, and all is as nothing compared to the benefit that comes from offspring, for if at the end of all generations a good, God-fearing man should issue from his loins, this is sufficient for him, since the Holy One, blessed be He, also created all the worlds for the sake of one righteous person, as it is written (Ecclesiastes 12:13), “Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man.” And if he worries because of the expense, this is a sign of little faith, for the Holy One, blessed be He, feeds and sustains from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice, and He gives bread to all flesh, bread according to the children.
Pele Yoetz 293:3: And how much more so if he has sons and not daughters, or daughters and not sons, so that he has not yet fulfilled the commandment of procreation, that he must employ every strategy in order to complete the fulfillment of the commandment of procreation. Go and learn from Leah our mother, that although she had four sons, when she stopped bearing, she went to great lengths, even bringing her maidservant into her house to be her rival, in order to merit building [her family] further. And Bilhah and Zilpah, who brought their rivals to their husbands, let all barren women be disciplined [to learn from them] and do as they did, that they should tell their husbands to take another wife in addition to them. And even though love is as fierce as death, jealousy of a rival is as hard as the grave, according to the pain is the reward, and she may be the cause that the Lord remember her as He remembered Sarah, Rachel, and Leah. And if she is not remembered, since these are the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge, in any case it shall be said of her (Isaiah 54:1), “Sing, O barren one,” for many are her children in the world of good understanding — how good is her portion and how pleasant is her lot.
Pele Yoetz 293:4: And it is known that the man is commanded regarding procreation and not the woman; therefore this commandment rests upon him to strive with all his effort to merit being built up [with children]. And if he has lived with his wife ten years and engaged in remedies and has not merited being built up, let him seek a way out and strive to appease her so that she grant him permission to marry another, or let him seek some Torah scholar to appease her with words that enter the heart. And she shall always remain the mistress of the house, for she is worthy of all the honor in the world for having brought her rival into her house. And thus let him stipulate with the other woman that she not anger her but rather honor her. And it is true that it is difficult to match them, for one woman is jealous of her fellow; therefore it is best that they be in two houses or two towns. And let him take even a poor woman for free, and even a lame one, and even a blind one, only to establish offspring. And if she does not agree, in any case let him sell all that he has and give it into her hand, and divorce her with a kosher writ of divorce, and take another, perhaps he will merit to be built up, for many have done so and succeeded. And even though the love of the wife of one's youth is fierce, all is as nothing compared to the love of the Creator and the love of one's own soul, for great is the evil of childlessness, as explained in the works citing the Talmud and Midrashim and the holy Zohar and the Sefer Chasidim — it makes a man's hair stand on end. And we must ask of our Father in Heaven that He not bring us and our offspring, nor any one of His people Israel, into such a difficult trial, and that He remember all the childless with lasting offspring for the service of the blessed Name.
Pele Yoetz 293:5: But if he comes into such a trial, let him gather strength to be a mighty man of valor before the Lord, to do what is fitting to do; according to the pain is the reward — he may yet see offspring, live long days, and the desire of the Lord shall prosper in his hand, and he shall rejoice in those who issue from his loins. And let not the man say, “Behold, I am a dry tree and this pain is mine alone,” if the matter is not as clear to him as the sun at noon, for this is not a way to remove him from transgression, nor does it exempt him from judgment, and in any case he must be concerned, for perhaps there is hope. And if, after all this toil and effort, he still does not merit to be built up, or he knows for himself that he is incapable of fathering children, then let him not be pained and let his heart not ache, since he has done what was incumbent upon him — behold, his reward is with him in full: “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5), for these are the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge, and to Him are events measured, and He does what is good in His eyes, for what does he need of sons and daughters except to do the will of our Father in Heaven — for the rest, the longing for children and for having heirs, is all vanity and vexation of spirit; and since he intended to perform a commandment and was prevented by circumstance beyond his control and did not perform it, Scripture accounts it to him as though he had performed it (Berachot 6a), and he receives good reward for his toil — why should he be pained? Let him rejoice in his portion and not add to his sorrow. And in any case, let him do what is in his power to do: let him raise an orphan boy and an orphan girl within his house, or the children of the poor devoted to Torah and Divine service, for Scripture accounts it to him as though he had fathered them (Sanhedrin 19b); or let him support some Torah scholar and provide sufficiently for his needs — he is considered like his son, as it is written (Psalms 77:16), “The sons of Jacob and Joseph, Selah.” And let him make consecrated endowments so that his name be remembered by them, and if he is a Torah scholar let him compose a book — whoever does these things acquires a good name, and for good his name shall be remembered, better than sons and daughters.
Pele Yoetz 293:6: And the essence of procreation in Torah is that he strive to originate novel insights, that his wellsprings be dispersed abroad, and that he raise up many students — perhaps he will merit that there be an offshoot of his plantings, the work of his hands in which to glory, and then happy is he, how good is his portion.
Pele Yoetz 294:1: Purim — Purim are festive days, remembered and observed, days of feasting and joy, joy of a commandment, for the Lord showed us extraordinary affection; for while we were standing at the feast of Ahasuerus, angering Him, and at that very time we became liable for having benefited from the feast of that wicked man (Megillah 12a), at that very moment the Merciful One had mercy upon us and provided the remedy before the affliction, for Vashti was killed, so that in the end the remedy sprouted forth from the feast of wine, and from this these days were established as days of feasting and joy. And we merited through it four commandments: the reading of the Megillah, feasting and joy, sending portions each man to his fellow, and gifts to the poor — these are beloved commandments that come from time to time, and their secret is exalted and lofty, and it is fitting to be especially careful with them to perform them properly, that is: the reading of the Megillah letter by letter, word by word, with clear speech and pleasant tune. And even one who does not know how to read it should press himself and seek, for a small fee, someone to read it with him, and proceed slowly, for those who rely on fulfilling their obligation merely by listening are quite likely not to fulfill their obligation, since it is almost impossible that they will not miss hearing a single word. And for this reason, if the reader has already fulfilled his own obligation and reads to make others — men or women — hear, it is not fitting to recite the blessing with [God's] Name and Kingship on their behalf, for one must be concerned lest they miss hearing a single word, in which case his blessing would be in vain. And it is known that women too are obligated in the commandments of this day like men, and must be careful to fulfill them properly.
Pele Yoetz 294:2: And regarding the commandment of feasting and joy, it is fitting to be careful to hold the main feast while it is still day, not as some are accustomed to do, holding the main feast at night. And one must drink somewhat more than is his usual custom, until he is somewhat merry, joyful and glad-hearted, with joy of a commandment, not the joy of frivolity like the custom of the frivolous who drink much wine until they lose their senses and do things that should not be done, and speak forbidden words of various kinds, causing the loss of the commandment of the afternoon prayer, and the biblically-mandated Grace after Meals, and the commandment of the evening prayer, saying that they do so for the sake of the commandment — but it is a transgression in their hand, for the Name did not command transgressing His commandments. Is it for the miracles and the redemption that this recompense is hoped for? Let this thing be uprooted and let there not be such a thing in Israel; rather, let Israel rejoice in its Maker with joy of a commandment, in measure, weight, and proportion, and let the drinking be according to the law of the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 294:3: And regarding the commandment of sending portions each man to his fellow, happy are the Israelites who fulfill it beyond the obligation; but how good it is to send to one for whom it means much, such as a great man sending to a lesser one, and to one who bears him a grudge, in order to gladden the heart of the wretched and revive the heart of the downtrodden, and to increase love and brotherhood, peace and friendship, for since he performs one commandment, he comes to perform another commandment. And likewise the commandment of gifts to the poor is fulfilled, but who takes it seriously enough to do it as it should be done, for “according to the camel is the burden” (Ketubot 67a). And the commandment of charity on this day surpasses that of other days, since the commandment of gifts to the poor accompanies it. And according to the secret of the matter, on Chanukah and Purim it is fitting to increase charity toward those who toil in Torah, for these days are, in secret, [the sefirot of] Netzach and Hod, which support the Torah, as explained in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory. And timing matters, for a commandment is beloved in its proper time, since for some time before Purim the poor borrow on the strength of the Purim collection, and after Purim expenses increase for the needs of Passover; behold, it is therefore fitting to have mercy on them and to reckon that the income should match the outlay, for the eyes of the poor are dependent on the wealthy, and the wealthy are dependent on the One who spoke and the world came into being — if one gives more, more is given to him; each according to the gift of his hand, the blessing of the Lord makes rich. Therefore let the weak say, “I am mighty,” to help the Lord among the mighty, and the Name shall help him.
Pele Yoetz 295:1: Pesach (Passover) — Pesach is an exceedingly holy festival, for had the Holy One, blessed be He, not brought our forefathers out of Egypt, we and our children would still be enslaved, a nation among a nation, and Torah and commandments would not have been given to us, and the name of Israel would not be remembered; and the Holy One, blessed be He, showed wondrous kindnesses to Israel, wondrously so, and showed them extraordinary affection, to a degree that no hand of ours can fully grasp, one part in a thousand thousand parts. We can only understand that He performed with us a kindness beyond investigation, and showed us His glory and His greatness and His love and His affection, the greatness of His ability to overturn the natural order, and His individual providence, in that He commanded us so extensively in His holy Torah in remembrance of the exodus from Egypt, and with every single commandment He mentions the remembrance of the exodus from Egypt. And He commanded us to make it a remembrance between our eyes and a sign upon our hand, and He gave us Sabbaths and festivals over which we say in the Kiddush, “in remembrance of the exodus from Egypt.”
Pele Yoetz 295:2: And the essence of remembering the exodus from Egypt every day, and the commandment of tefillin, is all so that the living take these matters to heart, in depth and breadth, and that Israel rejoice in its Maker and come to fear and love the honored and awesome Name, and cling to Him and serve Him with a whole heart, for so it is fitting after God has made known to us His love and affection and the greatness of His ability and the essence of His providence. And this is the reason our Maker commanded us on the night of Passover to increase the telling of the exodus from Egypt, and whoever increases the telling of the exodus from Egypt is praiseworthy. Besides that there are supernal secrets, and he builds his chambers in heaven and adds strength to the retinue on high, as explained in the language of the holy Zohar, Parashat Bo, that it kindles the heart and it is fitting to recite it on the night of Passover. There is also a reason according to the plain meaning: so that he increase the establishment in his heart and the hearts of his household members of love for the blessed God and fear of Him, for this is the whole of man. And this is the essence of the commandment of the telling, to relate to the members of his household in the telling of the exodus from Egypt how the Lord our God showed us His glory and His greatness, and His love and His compassion, and His ability and His providence, and that therefore it is fitting for us to serve Him with a whole heart and to keep all His commandments.
Pele Yoetz 295:3: And behold, on this holy festival the blessed Name sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us regarding the eating of matzah. And it is known that there is a dispute regarding the matter of “guarded” matzah: some say that it must be guarded from water touching it from the time of harvesting. And according to the opinion of the great halachic authorities, any matzah that is not guarded from the time of harvesting does not fulfill the obligation of eating matzah. And since the commandment of eating matzah is wondrous and its secret is exalted and lofty, raised on high, and it is called in the holy Zohar (part 2, p. 183) “the bread of healing,” for it is exceedingly effective for the healing of the soul — behold, therefore, let a man tremble and shrink back and be concerned for the opinion of those who say so, and not fail to make, at the very least, the guarded matzah he uses to fulfill the obligation of eating matzah from wheat guarded from the time of harvesting, for what advantage does a person have in all his toil that he toils for Passover if he does not fulfill the obligation of eating matzah. And even though there are those who say that he does fulfill his obligation, he should still be concerned for the opinion of the great halachic authorities.
Pele Yoetz 295:4: And there is already a parable for this: if one was sick, and ninety-nine doctors came and said that a certain remedy is beneficial for his healing, even though there is another remedy that is superior, better, and more effective, still this one is also beneficial; and another doctor comes, expert and skilled, and says that the remedy the other doctors mentioned is not beneficial and will harm the patient, and that the remedy they mentioned as the choicest is the only one beneficial for healing — who is such a fool and simpleton that he would not heed the opinion of the expert and skilled doctor, and would take the remedy that is beneficial according to everyone, and not take the remedy that might not help but rather harm? So it is with this matter. And because of this there are pious and men of action who are careful the entire Passover not to eat except matzah made from wheat guarded from the time of harvesting, in order to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions. For if on all other days it is fitting to be concerned to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions, how much more so regarding chametz and matzah, whose prohibition is exceedingly severe, carrying the penalty of karet, may the Merciful One save us, and one who is careful about it, his benefit is great. For it was written in the name of the Ari that one who is careful on Passover regarding the prohibition of chametz, and is concerned to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions, and is careful to the utmost degree of care, is assured that he will not sin the entire year — for this it is fitting to be exceedingly careful, for there is no reward greater than this. And this is why it is called “the bread of healing,” for it establishes faith and awe and love in the heart, and if a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be fitting and proper. And happy are the Israelites, and their wives even more than they, who are careful to remove the chametz to the utmost degree of care and are stricter than necessary — may the blessing of good come upon them. But the essential care is needed regarding what one puts into his mouth, that there be no concern whatsoever of leavening or admixture of chametz, and to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions.
Pele Yoetz 295:5: And it is fitting to station guards in the place where the matzot are made, that they scour the vessels well between each kneading, and that they not make thin wafers left lying about unattended, and afterward place many together on the peel [shovel] (called “shoifel”) and carry them to the oven, for if these things are not done, and it is a matzah that was kneaded with lingering water, this is eating chametz on Passover. And it is incumbent upon the leaders of the holy people to keep watchful eyes and fence in breaches and turn many back from sin and stand guard, so that they walk in the good way according to the Torah.
Pele Yoetz 295:6: And on the night the holy festival begins, let him gird himself with strength to fulfill the statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Pesachim 116b), that a person is obligated to see himself as though he himself went out of Egypt. And through constant pure thoughts his heart shall be kindled in such a way that he sees it is impossible not to rejoice, and according to his arousal and according to his deeds, so shall be his help from Heaven, for one who comes to purify himself is assisted [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a), that he rejoice in his Maker with abundant joy, joy of a commandment, as is fitting to do.
Pele Yoetz 295:7: And the kabbalists wrote that not only is the prohibition of chametz exceedingly severe during the days of Passover, but every matter of transgression is exceedingly severe, and does damage and makes an impression on Passover more and more than during the rest of the days of the year, and one must be careful and stand guard more than during all the rest of the days of the year.
Pele Yoetz 295:8: And behold, our sages, of blessed memory, arranged the order of the ceremonies of the night of Passover in the sequence “Kadesh U'Rechatz,” and now many of the common people do not know what it is, and it is fitting to go to a sage who will teach it to him, and to write it down in the vernacular as a reminder, in order to fulfill each item as is fitting to do. This is a great principle: “He who walks with the wise shall become wise” (Proverbs 13:20), and this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 296:1: Parnasah (Livelihood) — It is known that the key of livelihood is in the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He. He feeds and sustains all, from the horns of wild oxen to the eggs of lice, and gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness endures forever. Yet there is a distinction in the matter of livelihood, according to a person's deeds, and according to his fortune, and according to the knowledge of the God of knowledge. And these are the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge: there is one whose sustenance comes to him with ease and not with pain, with breadth and not with constraint, and wherever he turns he prospers and succeeds, and merits to become extraordinarily wealthy. And there is one who goes out to his work and his labor, rising early and staying late, traveling by sea and by river, toiling greatly, and yet eats the bread of sorrow, by the sweat of his brow eating scant bread and drinking measured water. And there is one who, after all the toil and effort, still must wander for bread and needs to be sustained from charity. “And the righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4), that he believe with complete faith that a person's sustenance is fixed for him from Rosh Hashanah (as they said, Beitzah 15b), and “nor bread to the wise, nor... the race to the swift” (Ecclesiastes 9:11) — rather, there are wise men who wander for bread, “and disgraces when he is satisfied” [a variant reading]; and the Name is the one who gives strength to do valiantly, and no person touches even a hairsbreadth of what is prepared for his fellow (Yoma 38b); therefore let him not resent nor create disputes if it seems to him that his fellow has cut into his livelihood, for judgment belongs to God, and even if he toils to grow rich all day and all night, one who increases does not gain more, and one who decreases loses nothing of what is fixed for him; and let the portion of the manna always be a remembrance before his eyes, kept as a sign for the children of Israel.
Pele Yoetz 296:2: And behold, it is known that there is a dispute in the Talmud (Berachot 35b): Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai held that a person must engage in Torah constantly, and his work is done by others, while Rabbi Yishmael held that one must conduct himself according to the way of the world. And the commentators explained that the words of both are true. And the resolution of the matter is that the pious, since they are pious, their work is blessed in a way beyond nature, and with the little they engage in work, the blessing of the Lord makes them rich; but for the rest of the people, the Holy One, blessed be He, sends their livelihood by natural means, and it is good to combine Torah study with an occupation, for Torah without an occupation ends in failure, etc. (Avot 2:2), and if there is no flour there is no Torah, and if there is no Torah there is no flour (ibid. 3:17). Behold, therefore, since we are, so to speak, orphans of orphans, we need to conduct ourselves according to the way of the world, and a person should go out to his work and his labor until evening, and let him do what is in his power to do, and let the good Name do what is good in His eyes.
Pele Yoetz 296:3: Only, even if the time presses him greatly and he has much business to attend to, he should not fail to pray the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers with the congregation, and to fix times for Torah study — both the one who does much and the one who does little — provided he does not let a day pass without it. And how good is the order of “Chok LeYisrael,” which is a fine order, containing everything — then the Lord shall command the blessing to be with him. But on Shabbatot, festivals, and the intermediate days of festivals, and whenever he is free, let him not turn to idleness, but rather engage in Torah. And let his business dealings be honest, and let him be careful and guard against every hint of prohibition, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven. And let him say thus with a full mouth every day:
Pele Yoetz 296:4: Behold, I am going to engage in business, and my trust is in the Name, that He will give me strength to do valiantly to earn a livelihood — for myself and the members of my household — in an honorable way, and to perform charity and acts of kindness, and so that I may fulfill all the commandments of my Creator properly; help us, God of our salvation, for the sake of the honor of Your Name; do not turn to our wickedness; deal with us in charity and kindness for the sake of Your great Name; may they be for favor, etc. And let not a day pass without giving charity according to his ability — this is a person's obligation. If he does thus, he shall trust in the Name of the Lord, and lean upon his God, that he be satisfied and full of the blessing of the Lord, and fulfill in himself the verse that is written (Psalms 128:2), “When you eat the labor of your hands, happy are you and it is well with you” — happy are you in this world, and it is well with you in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 296:5: And if the Lord has widened his boundary, let him diminish his business dealings, and let his work be done by others, and let him engage in Torah. And regarding this they said (Eruvin 54a), “If you have, benefit yourself.” And let him not be a stingy person who loves money, but rather let him rejoice in his portion and enjoy his toil, he and the members of his household, and let his flesh dwell securely and he shall live a life of tranquility, and let him send delicacies to the soul of his father and mother, and prepare delights for his own soul according to the blessing of the Lord which He has given him, for this is his portion from all his toil. But one who toils to grow rich through robbery, deceit, injustice, and falsehood, and encroachment upon another's boundary, and the like of the many prohibitions that arise in business dealings, and one who transgresses them because he does not stand on guard, and neglect of communal prayers, especially the afternoon prayer, which some neglect entirely, and neglect of Torah in that he does not fix any times for Torah at all — behold, this one has made his deeds evil and has cut into his own livelihood, and sees no sign of blessing in all his toil that he toils. And if for a time he prospers and “the way of the wicked prospers,” Scripture has already said (Jeremiah 17:11), “He who makes riches, but not by right, in the midst of his days shall leave them, and at his end shall be a fool.” And there is wealth kept by its owner to his harm — this is the deed of the [wicked] individual, who is made to prosper for a time through injustice and neglect of prayers and neglect of fixed times for Torah, in order to mislead him into persisting in his wickedness. But for one who walks in the way of the good, “the Lord tests the righteous” (Psalms 11:5), that he suffer loss and disquiet of spirit for a time, in order to test him and to benefit him in his end. But all who come into the world shall testify and declare that since the blessed Name is the one who gives strength to do valiantly, and He feeds and sustains all, it cannot be told that He gives more to transgressors of His will and they profit by transgressing His will, while to those who do His will He gives less and they suffer loss by doing the will of their Maker — this would be an unjust judgment even among flesh and blood, and far be it from God to be wicked, and from the Almighty to act unjustly; rather, the complete truth is as we have said. And all the people, to a person, know all this, and they believe it; only they are given over into the hand of their own inclination, and after knowing and hearing all this, there are those who do not abandon their evil custom and transgress against their own understanding and against their Maker's will, even though they know without doubt that it will not succeed, and that they are destined to give an account, and that there is good reward for the righteous in this world and the World to Come, and evil and bitter punishment for the wicked; nevertheless they do not gather strength to struggle with their inclination to walk in the way of the good and to do what is good and upright.
Pele Yoetz 296:6: But he who is a Jew shall take to heart that a person's coming into this world is only in order that he struggle with his inclination and subdue it, and thereby he gives satisfaction to his Maker and receives good reward for his toil in this world and the World to Come; and what advantage does a person have in his toil that he toils, if he labors to grow rich through prohibitions and neglect of prayers and commandments, knowing that it will not succeed, and that he is destined to give an account before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He? Therefore, let a man gather strength to struggle with his inclination, to do what is good and upright according to the Torah, and he shall be satisfied with good in this world, and shall delight in abundance for his soul in the World to Come, and this is the whole of man. And let him always seek mercy from the One to whom wealth belongs, for prayer accomplishes much. And every day let him pray for his livelihood in the blessing of “He who hears prayer,” and before every meal, as I have written above under the entry Achilah. And let him intend greatly in the blessings over enjoyments, and especially in Grace after Meals, to say them with intention, letter by letter, word by word, and let him intend greatly in the verse “You open Your hand,” for upon these the essence of livelihood depends.
Pele Yoetz 297:1: Pachad (Fear) — It is written (Job 3:25), “For the fear I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.” And it is written (Psalms 112:7-8), “His heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord; his heart is upheld, he shall not fear.” It follows that one who fears brings evil upon himself that would not otherwise have been fitting to come upon him, while “he who trusts in the Lord, kindness shall surround him” (Psalms 32:10). And it is true that a person has no control over his spirit, and even if they tell him all day, “Do not fear, do not fear,” he still fears; but a man can dispel his fear through deepening pure thoughts, reasoning: “Why should I fear the evils that occur in the world? Is it not better to fear the fear of the Name and the majesty of His glory?” And let him turn his fear away from his heart and turn his heart to other thoughts, for the heart cannot think two thoughts at once, and what benefit, what does it give, and what does it add to him that he fears? If a decree has been decreed upon him, it must inevitably come upon his head, for none can save from His hand; and if it has not been decreed upon him, his fear remains with him for nothing — and not only that, but it is possible that through his fear something will come upon him that was not decreed. Therefore let a person strengthen himself and let his heart be like the heart of a lion, trusting in the Name that no evil shall befall him; and if some decree has indeed been decreed upon him, whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good. And in any case, even though he should not fear, he should still be concerned and do what is in his power to do, and precede trouble with prayer, and give charity, which annuls the decree, and let the good Name do what is good in His eyes.
Pele Yoetz 297:2: But there is a fear that is good, as it is written (Proverbs 28:14), “Happy is the man who fears always,” and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 60a) that this is written regarding matters of Torah — that is, that his heart should always fear regarding Torah and commandments, lest he has not done what was fitting for him to do, and he should always say, “The journey is long and the provisions scant,” and fear lest his deeds not be accepted with favor before the King, exalted and lofty, according to the greatness of the obligation befitting him as a person, according to his ability and according to the severity that applies to him — and through this he shall ascend from level to level. For this is the evil of man on earth: that he is content with his portion and gives thanks for his portion and says, “Praise be to me, for I am a proper Jew; there is no murder, adultery, or theft in me; I only recite my prayer every day, and my righteousness answers for me, and I enjoy my own toil, and none of my labors will find in me any iniquity or sin.” And because of this, no man takes it to heart to ascend to higher levels, and no one regrets his own evil, for it seems to him that his deeds are pure and upright.
Pele Yoetz 297:3: And there was already an incident in the time of Maimonides, when a great man did not wish to confess on Yom Kippur, for he knew of himself that he had not committed any transgression, and why should he speak falsehoods before Him, blessed be He, whose seal is truth (Shabbat 55a)? And Maimonides answered him: “If you, the sincere one, knew how weighty is the service of the exalted Name, and how much is needed and fitting and required of the servant of this God and Master, you would certainly know that there is no day on which you do not do all that is stated in the confession, and even more besides. And every person is judged according to the greatness of his wisdom, for we find that King David, peace be upon him, had the sin of a married woman written against him, though she was in fact divorced (ibid. 56a); and so with every similar case — according to what the person is, so is his judgment and his standing, and even for the light matter you spoke of, you are destined to give an account,” until here his words. And regarding this, Mahari, of blessed memory, wrote in the book Lev David, [describing how] the listener, seeing the holy words of the father of the tradition, Maimonides, felt his sinews loosen and his knees knock together, beholding pleasantly the full weight of Heaven's judgment, and recognizing man's obligation in the order of service to our God, King of the world.
Pele Yoetz 298:1: Parshiyot (Torah Portions) — It is a known statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Berachot 8a), that a person should always complete his Torah portions along with the congregation, [reading] the Scripture twice and the Targum once, for whoever completes his portions with the congregation has his days and years lengthened. And behold, the essential commandment of reading the Scripture twice and the Targum once is on the sixth day [Friday], but for people occupied with earning their livelihood, it is better that they read it on Shabbat morning. And one who does not know how to read it should join with someone who knows how to read, and read it together. And the kabbalists wrote that one should be very exacting in reading the portion, Scripture twice and Targum once, reading it with all its cantillation and its grammatical precision, most thoroughly. And behold, regarding such a commandment, whose reward is stated alongside it — length of days is in its right hand — whoever is not concerned to fulfill it shall certainly be punished, whichever way you look at it: if he does not believe in the Torah and the words of the sages, he is judged in boiling excrement; and if he believes but is not concerned, and does not care for his own life, behold, he is liable for his own soul and is destined to give an account like one who destroys himself knowingly. And how much more so regarding a matter that is easy to fulfill — whoever does not desire life is likened to beasts. This is a great principle in Torah and in the fulfillment of the commandments; let the man who desires life take such things to heart, and out of doing it not for its own sake, he shall come to do it for its own sake, to give satisfaction before our Father in Heaven and to rectify matters at their root. For since the Torah portions are the utterances of His holiness, blessed be He, certainly there are wondrous supernal secrets in every single letter and every crown upon every letter, mountains upon mountains, and the whole Torah is entirely the names of the Holy One, blessed be He, and one who reads them builds his chambers in heaven (Amos 9:6); and even though we do not know, the reader reads in his own way, and let him consider that there are secrets and secrets of secrets, and “establish for us the work of our hands” (Psalms 90:17).
